title: Celestin's last illness and death
summary: Ridgley visited and prayed with Celestin, who said he would never pick up the horn again, and died of cancer.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah, he did well. Oh, he made money. He made dollars while I made pennies. He got no money when he was playing like when he was playing. He was a fine fellow. Good cornet player. Nice man. Good fellow. I tried to get him to quit playing. He wouldn't quit a little like this so much. I tell him, I said, son, you're getting so old. I said, you made a reputation out there, ain't I? I said, now you got a little bit of money. I said, I didn't have anything when I quit. I said, even my home was, the morris. I said, I didn't have anything. I didn't know what I was going to do. I didn't quit all the night. I said, I made it. I said, you can make it. I didn't do it. But I know he didn't like this so much. But the last words he said to me, I used to go down to the house on Grand Street. Go down there and I'd sing and I'd pray for him. He said, Ridley, if I ever get over there, I'll never pick up that horn again. I didn't say nothing in, but I thought. But he did that anyway. I said, I thought to myself too, but I used to tell him, I said, you old man? I said, you got a few dollars in my city. Got a little income? And I said, you can't keep on playing. And that dancing, going on like he was an old man and got seven years old and working hard all his life and all that. He didn't use, he said that people like it. I said, all right. So when they had him over here in the hospital, all the two damn mountain, he'd find out. And he sent for me, told the lady to come over there and pray for him. She told me, but this time of evening, I guess. I said, well, it's too late now. I was there first thing next morning. And he was there to see me and the doctor was so nice to him. I went in and I slept in a long while, I called him, and sang, prayed, and everything. And then when he went back down to his house, I did the bus and I used to get around there. And I would pray with him and do everything. But the last word he said, I heard him speak, he said, if I get over this, I'll never pick up that horn again. I thought too late because I knew that they had an outbreak on him, what's called a cancer. You see, because my wife.
I never knew what he died from. He said it, cancer. I didn't know.

My wife died. He canceled the blood. And I knew from the way that she said there was, you know, sakesing for her. And he told me, and they were doing the same thing with him, you see. And I said, they're looking for cancer. So I was in there and the doctor came in and said, they said, well, Selv, can I have you, old boy? And I said, he says, everything's all right, doctor? And the doctor said, yes. He said, we found out. He said, we found out.

That's what we want to find out about it." I said, yeah. He said, we're thinking we can do something right. The doctor said, only one little thing, Rick. He said, we got a little small operation. He said, it ain't much. He said, just a little operation when we get that. And I thought they had cancer. I said, I was sitting there. I said, cancer. Sighting for cancer. And sure enough, they operate on them next week. And after they operate on them, they send them home. And he told me when they were sending them home, they said, the doctor, when must I come back? So the doctor said, we'll send them for you. It was time. I thought again. Oh, he was suffering. He was suffering. He said he was sorry. He let them operate on them. And how did he get over it? Another couple days after he died.
